newsitem.title: UK: S&P sets Irish Intercontinental Bank CP ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P sets Irish Intercontinental Bank CP ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Thursday it assigned Irish Intercontinental Bank Ltd (IIB) A plus long-term and A1 short-term counterparty ratings.
"The outlook on the ratings is stable," S&P said in a statement.
S&P said the outlook reflected that of Kredietbank NV, IIB's parent.
"IIB should continue to enjoy the many tangible and intangible benefits of being part of a diversified international banking group," S&P said.
It said IIB's ratings reflected its position and role in the Kredietbank group (Kredietbank is currently rated AA minus/A1 by S&P) and its satisfactory fundamentals.

"Kredietbank owns 75 percent of the bank, while Irish Life Assurance hold the remaining 25 percent. In conformity with Irish banking regulations, a letter of comfort from Kredietbank has been supplied to the Central Bank of Ireland," S&P said.
It said IIB was a wholesale bank that serviced the Irish corporate sector with lending and treasury products.

"IIB is also involved in asset finance (an area in which the bank has made its most recent acquisition in the UK). Through the Dublin International Financial Services Centre (IFSC), IIB engages in a number of activities in conjunction with Kredietbank," said S&P.

"The IFSC is the centre for Kredietbank's global asset-backed trasactions (aircraft, shipping, and project finanace). IIB's retail side, mostly domestic mortgages through Irish Life Homeloans, is operated in conjunction with Irish Life," the agency said.
S&P said total assets of 1.7 billion Irish pounds and net income of 15.8 milion Irish pounds at year-end 1995 made IIB a niche player.
"Asset quality is good, reflecting the buoyant Irish economy and the bank's own strict credit standards, which are derived from those of Kredietbank," S&P said.

"Although the bank is rather dependent on the interbank market for its funding, it also has access to Kredietbank group companies that assist its liquidity, though it does not rely on this, expanding, for example, the proportion of its deposits from corporates."

"Capital levels are adequate for foreseeable growth in IIB's risk assets. It is notable that both shareholders have consistently been disposed to support IIB's expansion, most recently in November 1996 when they subscribed to an issue of 30 million Irish pounds of IIB perference shares," S&P said.
